note_tweet.text:
In 10 weeks, 4 AI labs shipped personal agents that never log off.
Most researchers will hand them the wrong jobs.

This month I finished my April travel reimbursements.
6 months late.

Federally funded PIs spend an estimated 44% of research time on admin.
ChatGPT cleared my pile in one sitting. 
Then it hit me. An always-on agent would never let the pile form.

What I'd tell any researcher setting one up:

1️⃣ Decide what it handles without telling you
↳ Do: easy to undo. Filing receipts.
↳ Digest: weekly. New papers.
↳ Ping: urgent and rare. A retraction of a paper you cite.
↳ Ask: anything sent in your name.

2️⃣ Every extra alert makes you likelier to miss the urgent one
↳ Clinicians override 49% to 96% of drug safety alerts.
↳ Keep the Ping lane tiny.

3️⃣ Literature updates don't need an always-on agent
↳ A scheduled weekly search in Claude or ChatGPT is enough.
↳ Keep your PubMed alert as a scheduled task (personal AI agents is overkill).

4️⃣ What it can see matters more than how smart it is
↳ Mine reads my personal Gmail, not my institutional inbox. Work email and patient data wait for institutional approval.
↳ Meta just paused Muse's chat sharing after about 6,800 shared links surfaced in public DNS records.

5️⃣ Start with a job where a mistake is easy to undo
↳ Receipts, filed by meeting as they arrive. You still press submit.

One catch: Dots aren't on ChatGPT Plus, and Claude Duet is a US waitlist. 

💬 Which admin job would you hand off first?

More on AI for academic research in my free newsletter (16,000+ researchers): https://t.co/XTq6dj6SoB

The media thought that was the story. It was not.

The underlying stack bypasses whole departments through xAI's own-computer model and always-on agents that maintain continuous state between conversations rather than resetting when the tab closes.
